claim: An attacker who obtains a shopper's session cookie replays it against the storefront API and places orders as that shopper.
notes: A stolen session cookie is replayed on an internet-facing endpoint; the canonical finding for this flow. The MFA gap is a separate weakness on the sign-in that issued the cookie: MFA raises the cost of obtaining one and does nothing about replaying one already taken, so a countermeasure here is binding or expiring the session rather than strengthening the login.

claim: An attacker POSTs a forged settlement webhook to the storefront API, impersonating the card processor to mark an unpaid order as paid.
notes: Callback authentication is unknown on an internet-facing endpoint; must be reported as unverified, not assumed present.

claim: An attacker positioned in the storefront tier modifies order contents in flight on the gRPC channel, whose transport protection is unverified.
notes: Crosses dmz to core with authentication none and encryption_in_transit unknown.

claim: An attacker with the shared full read/write database account alters order rows, changing prices or payment status directly.
notes: No least privilege: the same credential that reads can rewrite every row.

claim: A shopper denies having placed an order, and the receipt archive cannot contradict them because receipts record only the order service as the writer.
notes: The one audit record in the system carries the service identity, never the authenticated shopper.

claim: An attacker who reaches the database storage or its backups reads shopper addresses and card last-four, because protection at rest is unverified.
notes: encryption_at_rest is unknown on a store tagged pii and financial — report as unverified, and a needs-info verdict is acceptable here.

claim: An attacker with access to the internal network reads order contents and shopper identifiers off the gRPC channel, whose encryption is unverified.
notes: Same flow as the tampering entry; the lane difference is read versus modify.

claim: An attacker floods the unauthenticated settlement webhook endpoint until the storefront API stops serving shoppers.
notes: An internet-facing endpoint with no verified caller identity is the cheapest flood target in the model.

claim: An attacker who extracts the fleet-wide pre-shared key from any one node publishes readings to the gateway as any other device in the fleet.
notes: The defining finding of this case: one shared, never-rotated key across physically exposed devices. The attacker holds a key they were not issued, which is use-credential rather than impersonate.

claim: An attacker with physical access presents themselves as a field technician on the node's serial console, whose authentication is unverified.
notes: Physical exposure is stated in the source; console authentication is unknown, so it must be reported unverified.

claim: An attacker who can write to the firmware bucket plants a malicious image that every polling node installs, since image signature verification is unverified.
notes: Fleet-wide code execution; the source explicitly flags signature checking as unknown.
note: Bucket write access is required. The finding does not specify how the writer obtained or exercised it.

claim: A customer disputes a reading attributed to their site and no per-device identity exists to establish which node actually sent it.
notes: Follows directly from a fleet-wide rather than per-device credential.
note: The shared fleet key defeats per-device attribution regardless of who disputes the reading.

claim: An attacker who obtains a read grant on the telemetry lake reads customer site addresses and occupancy patterns, and nothing records who holds that grant or whether protection at rest would stop a raw copy.
notes: Occupancy data is unusually sensitive: it reveals when a physical site is empty.

claim: An attacker on the path between a node and the gateway reads readings and the presented key, because transport encryption on the MQTT session is unverified.
notes: The same wire carries the credential and the data; a needs-info verdict on encryption is acceptable.

claim: An attacker floods the internet-exposed MQTT broker with connections until genuine nodes can no longer publish readings.
notes: The gateway is the single ingest point for the whole fleet.

claim: An attacker who obtains a partner's never-rotated static SFTP key uploads extracts as that partner.
notes: Long-lived shared secret held by a third party; the primary identity weakness on the ingest path. The attacker holds a key they were not issued, which is use-credential rather than impersonate.

claim: An attacker deposits a file into another partner's folder and the scheduler processes it as that partner's extract, because it never checks the depositor.
notes: Stated absence, not an unknown: the source says the check does not happen. Attribution of data to a source is the whole point of the folder layout.

claim: An attacker who can write to the landing bucket alters claim records before the nightly run, and only the schema is checked before they reach the warehouse.
notes: Content validation is stated as absent; the case's headline integrity finding.
note: The finding requires a write to the landed records but specifies no route to that write.

claim: An analyst who needs only aggregate figures reads member names and dates of birth, because the grant covers the whole dataset.
notes: Stated absence of column-level restriction over health data; the highest-likelihood disclosure in the model.

claim: An attacker who reaches the Airflow metadata database recovers every partner key and connection string it holds, since its protection at rest is unverified.
notes: Single store concentrating credentials for the entire ingest path.

claim: An attacker deposits an enormous or malformed file that consumes the nightly window and prevents genuine extracts from being processed.
notes: The batch shape is the vulnerability: a missed window is a lost day, not a slow request.

claim: An attacker who obtains a calling team's API key calls the inference gateway as that team for as long as the key stays valid, and no key has ever been expired.
notes: Bearer credential on an internet-facing endpoint. No key has ever been expired, so how long a stolen one stays valid is unverified.

claim: Any workload inside the model network submits inference requests posing as the gateway, which the model server accepts on network position alone.
notes: Stated absence of authentication behind a boundary that is only 'meant to be' closed.

claim: An attacker who can write to the registry swaps the model artifact and the model server loads it without any integrity verification.
notes: The defining supply-chain finding of this case; the source states verification is absent.
note: Replacing the registry artifact requires write access. The claim leaves the writer's position open.

claim: An attacker with model-network access writes to the unauthenticated Redis feature store and changes the features a decision is made on.
notes: No password is a stated fact, not an unknown; poisoning features silently changes inference output.

claim: An attacker who obtains a read grant on the inference log reads the raw end-user prompts the source says it retains, and nothing records who holds that grant.
notes: A debugging store that silently became the most sensitive data collection in the system.

claim: An attacker with model-network access reads per-customer account age and spend bands from the unauthenticated feature store.
notes: Stated absence of authentication over data tagged pii and financial.

claim: A caller holding a valid key floods the gateway with inference requests and exhausts the shared GPU capacity behind it.
notes: GPU capacity is the scarce, expensive resource; no quota or rate limit per key is described.

claim: An attacker interacts with the web application as a legitimate user, because how the application authenticates the browser is unverified.
notes: Authentication on the one internet-crossing flow is unknown; needs-info is an acceptable verdict, silence is not.

claim: An attacker who reaches the queue enqueues jobs as if they came from the web application, since queue authentication is unverified.
notes: The queue is the trust hand-off in this design; nothing states how a producer is identified.

claim: An attacker who can write to the web application config changes the queue endpoint or credentials and redirects the application's work.
notes: Config stores are control planes; protection on this one is entirely unstated.
note: Changing the config is the prerequisite. The claim does not distinguish a config interface from local access.

claim: An attacker who compromises the background worker reads the database credentials from its config store.
notes: This is the threat the original cookbook model records against this element; protection at rest is unstated.

claim: An attacker who compromises the internet-facing web application reads the queue credentials from its config store.
notes: Same shape as the worker finding, but reachable from the internet-facing tier, so likelier.

claim: An attacker floods the queue with jobs until the worker cannot keep up and queued work stops completing.
notes: A single worker behind an unbounded queue; the backlog is invisible to the user who submitted the work.

claim: An attacker connects to the exposed lobby port as another player, because how the lobby authenticates a client is unverified.
notes: An internet-exposed port with unknown authentication is the highest-signal fact in the model.

claim: An attacker connects directly to a game server on its exposed port, bypassing the lobby, as a player who was never assigned to that match.
notes: The direct client-to-server path is a second entry point that skips whatever matchmaking establishes.

claim: A player modifies the game client on their own machine and sends manipulated gameplay actions that the servers accept.
notes: The defining threat of this domain: the client runs on hardware the operator explicitly does not control, so client-side state is attacker-controlled input.
note: The player modifies the modeled game client on a host they control and uses that client's channel to send the actions.

claim: An attacker alters match statistics in the stats database to change rankings or rewards.
notes: Competitive integrity is the business asset; write authentication on this path is unverified.
note: The claim specifies altered statistics but no access mechanism.

claim: An attacker who reaches the player database reads player account data, whose protection at rest is unverified.
notes: Report as unverified; needs-info is an acceptable verdict given the model states nothing.

claim: An attacker on the network path reads matchmaking and gameplay traffic, if either client link carries anything confidential over a segment they can observe; the model records the two links as bare port numbers and no transport protection either way.
notes: Both links are recorded as bare port numbers — the model gives no transport protection at all.

claim: An attacker floods the exposed lobby until players can no longer be matched into games.
notes: The lobby is a single chokepoint that every session passes through.

claim: An attacker floods a game server's exposed port and disrupts a match in progress for every player in it.
notes: Directly reachable match servers are the domain's signature availability problem; a disrupted match cannot be retried.

claim: An attacker who gets access to the moderation website acts on player accounts with whatever authority it holds over the player database, which the source records as direct read and write and never bounds by role or by account.
notes: No role separation inside the tool is described; the blast radius is the whole player base.
note: Access to the moderation tool is required. The claim does not say whether the attacker uses a support account or controls the tool itself.

claim: An attacker who can reach a game server sends it a match hand-over of their own making, choosing who is in the match and under which player identifiers, if the game server checks nothing about the caller or the hand-over; the source records no authentication on that link.
notes: Provenance: own-list 06.4, 2026-09-21; drafted by the maintainer on 2026-09-22. The list preceded the full marks set but followed exposure to earlier corpus findings; it was not blind. The lobby-to-server handover is explicit; authentication and handover validation are unspecified. Reachability of a game server does not itself establish access to an accepted handover interface. Distinct from player-facing impersonation.

claim: An attacker holding the shared build token calls the deploy controller as if it were the build runner and names an image sha of their own choosing as the current release.
notes: The one credential the source describes in full, and it describes it as shared across every pipeline and never rotated. Holding it is indistinguishable from being the runner.

claim: An attacker on the retail WAN presents itself to the image registry as a store server and pulls the estate's container images, if the registry identifies a puller no better than the source records a store being identified, which is not at all.
notes: The source says the registry allows the pull and that nobody has written down what a store server presents to it; needs-info is the right verdict, not silence.

claim: An attacker publishes a package that the lockfile resolves to and the runner bakes it into the image unchecked, because signatures on downloads are not verified.
notes: A stated absence, not an unknown — the source says outright that the runner does not verify signatures, so this is grounded rather than needs-info.

claim: An attacker replaces the image stored under a commit-sha tag in the registry, so store servers pull attacker content while the recorded release is unchanged.
notes: Worth keeping separate from the controller-record claim: this one leaves the release record honest, so nothing in the described system would show a change.
note: The tag must be overwritten, but the claim does not specify how the attacker writes to the registry.

claim: The deploy controller cannot tell which pipeline set a release, because every pipeline presents the same shared build token.
notes: High likelihood because it is not an attack condition but the described steady state — the token is stated to be the same for every pipeline.
note: The shared token obscures which pipeline acted even during ordinary authorized deployments.

claim: An attacker who reads wherever the build runner keeps the shared build token recovers it and can thereafter set the estate's release; the source states the runner presents the token and never says where it is kept.
notes: Recovering the credential is a separate action from using it, and the corpus files the use under spoofing; the never-rotated qualifier is what makes recovery durable.
note: The token's storage location and the means of reading it are explicitly unspecified.

claim: An attacker who compromises the build runner controls what every store server runs, because the runner both writes the image and holds the token that names the release.
notes: The runner concentrates both halves of the deploy path, so the build environment is effectively a higher-privilege zone than the estate it feeds.

claim: An attacker holding the signing key mints a token for any staff id carrying any groups, and every application accepts it as a genuine sign-in.
notes: The source states one key signs the tokens for every application, so the key is the whole authorization system and not merely one application's.

claim: An attacker who obtains a colleague's token acts as that colleague for the rest of its twelve hours, because nothing calls back to the broker and there is no way to pull a token back.
notes: Two stated qualifiers compound here, and neither is an unknown; the twelve-hour window is the stated blast radius of every other spoofing claim in this case.

claim: An attacker writes a group into the broker's directory and the next token issued to that colleague carries it into every application.
notes: The directory is where authorization actually lives in this design; writing to it grants durable authority without touching a key or a token.
note: A directory write is required, but the route by which the attacker changes the group is unspecified.

claim: A franchise sign-in cannot be attributed to a person, because the identity was asserted by a provider we do not run and whether the log covers that route at all is unverified.
notes: The source raises the franchise coverage question itself, which is the clearest signal in the text that this is the attribution gap worth reporting.
note: The logging gap applies to the franchise sign-in regardless of who initiated it.

claim: An attacker who reaches the key store reads the signing key, if the store hands out the private half rather than only signing with it and protection at rest does not stop them; the source records neither.
notes: Recovering the key is a separate action from using it, and the corpus files the use under spoofing; one key for every application is what makes the recovery worth this severity.
note: The private key must be extractable. The claim does not establish whether the attacker calls a store interface, controls a reader or obtains the stored bytes.

claim: An attacker makes the broker unavailable and no colleague can sign in to anything, because everything colleagues use signs them in through it.
notes: The source's first sentence states the single point of failure, and the twelve-hour token is the only thing that softens it for colleagues already signed in.
note: The claim specifies the broker outage but gives no mechanism for causing it.

claim: A colleague who is a store manager in one store changes prices and voids transactions in every store, because the console decides from the group alone and never checks which store they belong to.
notes: The case's signature claim and the only one the source states as a completed fact rather than as a gap. High likelihood because no attacker step is required: a legitimate token already carries the authority.

claim: A leaver keeps their access until the nightly pull runs, and a token issued before it goes on working for twelve hours after that.
notes: Three stated facts compound into one window — nightly removal, twelve-hour tokens, no revocation — and no single sentence of the source contains it, which is what makes it the hardest claim in this case to reach.

claim: An attacker submits orders to the web API as if they came from the mobile app, since how the API authenticates callers is unverified.
notes: The source states outright that nobody can say what the API does about authentication, and the app is the only stated client; needs-info is an acceptable verdict here, silence is not.

claim: An attacker who obtains a copy of the catalogue spreadsheet sends SQL to the web API as the catalogue tool, if the file carries whatever the API accepts as that tool's identity; the source never says what that is.
notes: The macro path's authority is carried by a file on a laptop; nothing in the source identifies who is driving it.

claim: An attacker on the network path alters order details in flight between the app and the web API, because that traffic runs over plain HTTP.
notes: The missing TLS is stated by the source rather than inferred, so this is the one claim in the case that rests on no unknown at all.

claim: An attacker drives the spreadsheet's macros to change catalogue prices through the web API.
notes: The stated purpose of the path, exercised by the wrong party; distinct from injecting statements the path was never meant to carry.
note: Operating the macros is required. The claim does not specify the operator's account or require code execution in the spreadsheet process.

claim: An attacker appends further SQL to the statements the macros send so the web API executes changes beyond prices and product copy, if the API passes what it receives to the database without restricting it to those statements; the source says only that the macros speak SQL to it.
notes: Injection through a path that carries statements rather than parameters; kept distinct from the price-change claim because the target differs. `inject` against a claim about altering a price is a verb difference as well as an element one.

claim: An attacker on the network path reads customer details out of the app's plain-HTTP traffic to the web API.
notes: The clearest finding in the case and the one that needs no unknown; a run that misses it has not read the source at all.

claim: An attacker who reaches the user database reads customers' names, addresses and the cards they paid with, since at-rest protection is unverified.
notes: The source names the contents and then says outright that nobody knows whether the store is encrypted.

claim: The confirmation fax discloses a customer's name and address to whoever holds the dialled number, because nobody checks it arrived at the right place.
notes: The case's signature threat and the reason the fax leg is in the corpus at all: a channel where the control is not unverified but unavailable, which is a different thing from unknown.
note: The wrong recipient gets the fax through normal delivery. No attacker's interface access or on-path interception is required.

claim: A customer sends the web API the catalogue operations the marketing spreadsheet sends, changing prices and product copy, if the API decides what a caller may do no more finely than it decides who the caller is; the source says the macros speak SQL to the same API the app calls and records no role separation.
notes: Provenance: own-list 09.5, 2026-09-21; drafted by the maintainer on 2026-09-22. The list preceded the full marks set but followed exposure to earlier corpus findings; it was not blind. Conditional role-authorization bypass on the shared API. Distinct from posing as the catalogue tool at reference 1 and accessing customer records through that tool at reference 17. No role-check implementation is stated.

claim: An attacker holding the admin's database credentials connects to MySQL as the admin from anywhere on the internet, since there is no jump host in the way.
notes: The source states the path is reachable from wherever the admin happens to be, which is the same as saying it is reachable from wherever an attacker happens to be.

claim: An attacker publishes assets into the CDN bucket as if they came from the web server, if the push accepts a writer it does not authenticate, which the source leaves unverified.
notes: The source says outright that nothing tells you how the push is authenticated; this is the unknown the case is built around.

claim: An attacker on the network path rewrites a stylesheet or script in flight before it reaches the reader, because assets are fetched over plain HTTP.
notes: The mixed-transport trap: the page arrives over HTTPS and its executable furniture does not, so the protection on the origin link buys nothing.

claim: An attacker who can write to the CDN bucket replaces a published asset and every reader of the site loads it.
notes: Planting the artifact at rest, kept distinct from modifying it in transit: `plant` against `alter-in-transit` on one artifact, which element agreement alone would merge.
note: The attacker must replace a stored asset. The claim does not specify how they obtain write access.

claim: An attacker on the network path modifies the admin's statements in flight, because the connection carries no TLS.
notes: The missing TLS is stated rather than inferred, and the traffic it protects is database administration.

claim: An attacker sniffing the admin's unsecured MySQL connection reads account and comment records in clear text.
notes: The single highest-signal finding in the case: a stated absence of TLS on a link stated to carry the whole database.

claim: An attacker who can write to the CDN bucket plants an asset there — a stylesheet or a download, which is what the source says the CDN serves — and the site delivers it to every reader as its own, because nothing records how the push to the bucket is authenticated.
notes: Where the two crossings compound: write access in a zone the site does not control becomes content the site vouches for, and neither crossing on its own carries that. The source names images, stylesheets and downloads on this path and no script, so what the reader's browser then does with the asset is not settled here.
note: The attacker must plant the asset, but the claim leaves open how the writer gains bucket access.

claim: A commenter submits content that the CMS keeps and later serves to other readers, and their browsers treat it as markup or script rather than text, if nothing encodes or sanitizes a comment on the way out; the source says the database holds comments and states no such handling.
notes: Provenance: own-list 10.10, 2026-09-21; drafted by the maintainer on 2026-09-22. The list preceded the full marks set but followed exposure to earlier corpus findings; it was not blind. Stored comments are explicit; serving attacker-controlled comments to another reader and unsafe rendering remain prerequisites. A prior reference claim is not independent evidence of rendering behavior. Context-appropriate encoding or sanitization may prevent execution.
note: The commenter supplies content through the site's comment interface. The claim does not require an authenticated account.

claim: An attacker signs in to the scheduling web app as a colleague and reads that colleague's shifts and details, if colleague authentication does not stop them, which is unverified.
notes: The source explicitly says nobody has documented how colleagues sign in. needs-info is the right verdict here; silence is not.

claim: An attacker signs in as a store manager and builds that store's rota, if manager authentication does not stop them, which is unverified.
notes: Same unknown as the colleague lane but a materially higher impact, which is why the two are kept as separate references rather than one.

claim: An attacker presents itself to the file share as the payroll system and collects the weekly payroll export, if the share does not identify and authorize a collector, which is unverified.
notes: The export is sensitive, so who collects it is a question the source does not answer. The check is on the collector's identity and authorization, not on which zone either side sits in.

claim: An attacker with a write path to the file share alters the payroll export while it sits there, and the payroll system collects hours nobody worked if it checks the file no further.
notes: The export rests unattended between two independent trust zones, and nothing states any integrity control over it. This is the case's strongest finding.
note: The export must be writable before pickup. The claim does not specify how the writer reaches it.

claim: An attacker reads colleague names, contact details and availability from the rota database, because whether it is encrypted at rest is unverified.
notes: The source states what the data is but never classifies it. The pii tag comes from the content, and data_classification stays unknown; a case that conflates the two is exactly what this case is here to catch.

claim: An attacker with access to the file share reads a whole store's payroll export in one file.
notes: Aggregation is the point: the export concentrates in one artifact what the database holds per colleague.

claim: An attacker who can stop the scheduling service writing the weekly export leaves the payroll system with no hours to collect, and nothing records what a pay run does when the export is absent.
notes: A weekly batch with a deadline behind it fails differently from a request path: the damage is a missed pay run, not slow pages.
note: Preventing the export is sufficient. The claim specifies no particular way of doing so.

claim: A colleague uses the shared app to build or change a rota as though they were a store manager, if the app does not enforce the separation between the two roles, which is unverified.
notes: Both roles are stated to use the same app, and no authorization rule between them is stated anywhere. This is the finding that follows from the shared-app fact rather than from any missing control.

claim: An attacker who obtains a supplier's vendor-issued password signs in as that supplier and uploads paperwork in their name, if the password alone admits them; whether a second factor or another access control stands in the way is unverified.
notes: Sign-in is the one control the source actually states, so this claim rests on a stated fact rather than on an unknown. Whether a second factor exists is never stated, and asserting its absence would be unsupported. The attacker holds the supplier's password, which is use-credential rather than impersonate.

claim: An attacker signs in to the portal as a category manager and approves supplier paperwork, if manager sign-in does not stop them; the vendor's datasheet asserts that all access is fully authenticated and the source records nothing about how a manager signs in.
notes: The datasheet's fully authenticated and audited covers this flow rhetorically and states nothing about it. An analyst that treats the manager path as authenticated because the vendor says so has swallowed the claim.

claim: An attacker writes a file into the landing bucket while posing as the vendor's nightly push, if the bucket does not authenticate and authorize the writer, which is unverified.
notes: The one flow crossing from the vendor platform into our cloud account, and the source states no authentication on it at all.

claim: An attacker modifies the extract file in the landing bucket before the supplier master service loads it, and the altered supplier records reach the database.
notes: The runbook states the file is picked up as-is, which is a stated absence of validation rather than an inferred one — the strongest grounded finding in the case.
note: The loaded file must be altered. The claim does not specify a writer identity or an access path.

claim: An attacker on the path of the nightly push alters the extract in transit, if that channel protects its integrity no further, which the source leaves unresolved.
notes: This is the case's central reference. The correct handling of we were told it is encrypted end to end against the runbook's plain CSV is needs-info on an unresolved question; the first names no layer and the second describes the file at rest, so neither settles the channel. Both a confident encrypted and a confident unencrypted are wrong, and the latter is worse.

claim: An attacker who obtains a read grant on the landing bucket reads the whole supplier extract, which the runbook says arrives as a plain CSV; nothing records who holds that grant or how the bucket is protected at rest.
notes: Enterprise-grade encryption throughout is a claim about the vendor's platform; the bucket is in our cloud account and the source says nothing about it either way.

claim: An attacker stops the nightly extract from being loaded and the supplier database silently keeps serving stale supplier records.
notes: The failure here is staleness rather than an outage: nothing in the source detects a missing nightly file.
note: The claim depends on a missed load and gives no mechanism for stopping it.

claim: A signed-in supplier reaches another supplier's compliance documents through the portal, if the portal does not authorize access per tenant, which the source does not state either way.
notes: Many suppliers share one vendor-hosted product and the source states nothing about isolation between them. Fully compliant is the phrase most likely to be mistaken for an answer to this.

claim: A signed-in supplier invokes a category manager's review action and approves their own compliance paperwork if the portal fails to enforce reviewer authorization on that action.
notes: Provenance: own-list 12.3, 2026-09-21; drafted by the maintainer on 2026-09-22. The list preceded the full marks set but followed exposure to earlier corpus findings; it was not blind. Authentication does not establish reviewer authorization. Role enforcement is unknown, not shown absent. Distinct from cross-supplier document access at reference 13.

claim: A vendor whose platform an attacker controls pushes a nightly extract on the genuine channel carrying supplier records that are false, and the supplier master service writes them into the supplier database, if nothing on our side checks a record against anything but the file it arrived in; the source describes no such check.
notes: Provenance: own-list 12.7, 2026-09-21; drafted by the maintainer on 2026-09-22. The list preceded the full marks set but followed exposure to earlier corpus findings; it was not blind. Authentic delivery can carry false records from a compromised vendor. Distinct from vendor impersonation at reference 2. Feasible independent validation and reconciliation depend on the records; no such controls are described. Vendor marketing is not proof of compromise or missing controls. The elements name the master service and the supplier database rather than the vendor and the landing bucket, because the finding is that nothing validates a record that arrived authentic, and that is where such a record lands. On the bucket this claim keyed to an identity the reader marked `duplicate` on 2026-09-21, against a dropped claim about an *unauthorized* writer; an identity check answers that one and passes this one, so the mechanisms differ and the place has to say so.

claim: An attacker who holds the importer's never-rotated API token posts work orders to the dispatch API as the importer.
notes: The token is the case's one fully stated credential: issued once at build time and never rotated. It is also the only stated authentication on any crossing into the control plane, so a lane that misses it is reading nothing the source gave it.

claim: An attacker opens a WebSocket to the dispatch API in a duty engineer's name, because nothing states what the handshake checks.
notes: The source states the handshake's authentication was never written down, which is an unknown somebody registered rather than a topic nobody raised.

claim: An attacker who can supply the hourly pull with a document it accepts returns XML that plants work orders the partner never sent, if the control plane turns that document into orders unchecked.
notes: The path the case is built on: a document from outside becomes work the control plane hands to a depot, and nothing between the two checks it.

claim: An attacker on the corporate network alters a dispatch request on its way into the control plane, because nothing states the call is encrypted.
notes: encryption_in_transit is unknown on the one flow that carries crew moves, and the crossing it makes is into the privilege zone.

claim: An attacker on the corporate network reads the live job status stream, because nothing states the WebSocket runs over TLS.
notes: The transport of the long-lived channel is the attribute the source explicitly leaves unwritten.

claim: An attacker who obtains a copy of the dispatch database reads the crew names and mobile numbers in it.
notes: The contents are stated and the at-rest protection is stated to be unwritten, so pii comes from the content while data_classification stays unknown.

claim: An attacker holds open enough WebSockets to the dispatch API that duty engineers lose live job status.
notes: A long-lived channel is the availability shape a request-response API does not have, and the API serves both the console and the importer.

claim: An attacker gets a duty engineer's browser to dispatch a crew from a page the attacker controls, if the browser attaches the engineer's session to a cross-site request the API accepts and the API checks nothing beyond it, none of which is recorded.
notes: The browser holds authority the corporate laptop does not, so a request it is made to send spends the control plane's rights. CORS is not the write authorization: the prerequisites are credential attachment, a method and content type the API accepts, and no further validation of the request, and none of the three is recorded.

claim: An attacker-controlled page uses a duty engineer's browser to read dispatch information through the engineer's authority, which over HTTP requires the browser to attach usable credentials and the API to permit credentialed response access from the attacker's origin, and over WebSocket requires usable session credentials on the handshake and acceptance of the attacker's origin without effective authorization against cross-site use.
notes: Provenance: own-list 13.2 and 13.3, 2026-09-21; drafted by the maintainer on 2026-09-22. The list preceded the full marks set but followed exposure to earlier corpus findings; it was not blind. Maintainer merged own-list 13.2 and 13.3; both flow IDs are retained. HTTP CORS response permissions do not govern WebSocket handshakes. Credential attachment, browser reachability and the relevant origin checks are separate prerequisites. Authentication and data returned are unspecified. Distinct from reference 16's forged state-changing request. In either case the browser must reach the internal API, and the response or stream must expose the information; that shared prerequisite sits here rather than in the claim, which the 500-character bound on the field caps.

claim: An attacker who controls a URL that begins with a partner's registered redirect URI has the authorization server send members' authorization codes to it.
notes: The case's stated OAuth defect: prefix matching on redirect URIs, so the authorization server itself sends the code to a URL the attacker owns. A confidential partner still needs its secret to redeem the code, which caps the impact.

claim: A member denies approving a gift-card redemption a partner app made in their name, and the ledger cannot show that they approved it, because it records the client and not the member.
notes: Stated outright. The consent screen proves a member connected the app once; it proves nothing about any one redemption.

claim: Anyone who can read the API log store collects the bearer access tokens it records and uses them before they expire.
notes: Stated outright: every request is written with its headers. The tokens are plain bearer tokens that live an hour and carry every scope for partner apps, so a log reader holds live credentials.
note: The token is exposed to anyone who can read the log. The claim does not specify how they read it.

claim: A partner app that only needs to show a member's points redeems that member's points for gift cards, because every partner app holds every scope.
notes: Stated outright: every partner gets every scope. Redemption needs nothing beyond the scope, so the grant a partner legitimately holds reaches money.

claim: An attacker who guesses or reuses a company admin's password signs in to the billing app as that admin, because there is no second factor.
notes: Stated outright: password only, for admins too. An admin can change the company's payout bank account.

claim: A company user posts an invoice edit that sets the paid flag or replaces the company's payout bank account, and the billing app saves it because it saves every field it receives.
notes: Stated outright. A viewer can do it too unless the app checks the role on the request, which the source says nobody wrote down. The bank account is the payment page's bank account, so payers then pay the attacker.

claim: A support agent acting as a customer user changes that company's invoices, and the database record names only the customer user, not the agent.
notes: Stated outright: everything the agent does is recorded against the customer user.

claim: Anyone steps through invoice numbers on the payment page and reads every company's invoices, company names and bank details, because the numbers count up across all companies and the page asks for no sign-in.
notes: The case's clearest cross-tenant finding, and entirely stated: a shared counting sequence and a page with no sign-in.

claim: A signed-in user of one company opens another company's invoice by its number, if the billing app does not check that the invoice belongs to the user's company.
notes: Conditional on the check nobody wrote down. The tenant filter lives in each query by hand and the database has no row-level security, so one missed filter is enough.

claim: A user asks for PDFs as often as they like and fills the render queue, so the one-job-at-a-time renderer delays every other company's PDFs.
notes: Stated outright: no limit on requests, one job at a time, one renderer for all companies.

claim: A viewer sends the requests behind the buttons the pages hide from them and performs admin actions, if the billing app does not check the role on each request.
notes: Conditional on the check nobody wrote down; hiding a button is the only stated control.

claim: If the lending API does not authenticate calls from the app, an attacker borrows, renews or reserves books as another member.
notes: The hedge this case exists for. Priya's answer about the token is a hedge, so authentication is unknown and the finding is conditional. An extraction that records the hedged token as the value suppresses this finding.

claim: A loan closed by hand or a block cleared at the desk cannot be traced to a person or a branch, because every desk shares one login and the history records only that the change was made by hand.
notes: Stated outright, twice: the shared login, and that nobody can tell who or which branch. The finding with the strongest grounds in the case.
note: Every manual change under the shared login has the same attribution gap, whoever operated the desk.

claim: An attacker floods the lending API with calls, and no member or kiosk can borrow or return anything, because ordinary launch-day load already took the one service down twice.
notes: The source states this failure already happened twice last summer under legitimate load alone, and that every kiosk and every phone depends on the one API.

claim: If a member or unauthenticated caller can reach the API's manual-return, block-clearing or extension operations and the API fails to enforce staff authorization, that caller could perform staff-only changes.
notes: The transcript puts the lending API on the internet, and the circulation page and the app's calls reach one API. Neither source states which operations a call from outside the branch network can reach, or a staff role check. An extraction that believes the superseded note and writes internal removes the internet caller from this finding.
note: The claim expressly covers both a signed-in member and an unauthenticated caller.

claim: A desk worker marks an unreturned book as returned, clears a justified block or grants an improper extension on purpose, through the circulation page, with the powers the desk already has.
notes: Desk staff hold these powers by the note, so this is misuse of a grant, not an escalation. The shared login stops the change being traced to a person or a branch, which is the repudiation claim on the same flow.
